summary: The article profiles six treasured family desserts and the baking secrets behind them, from a cherry pie on Nostrand Avenue to apple dumplings in the Appalachian foothills. Each recipe is tied to a family member and a specific technique or ingredient, such as almond extract, 70% cocoa chocolate, precise ratios, blackstrap molasses, overnight soaking, and Granny Smith apples. It presents these desserts as living heritage that bonds generations.
one_line: A feature on six family heirloom desserts and the secret techniques and ingredients that families have passed down through generations.
key_facts: Since September 1, 2023, Regional Cuisine and Recipes has been unveiling treasured family desserts and baking secrets.
Grandma Rose's cherry pie is baked by Julia Cartwright, a third-generation baker, in the Cartwright family kitchen on Nostrand Avenue.
Rose Anderson penned her cherry pie secret in 1956: a tablespoon of almond extract and a dash of cinnamon added to the traditional filling.
Uncle Moe's molten chocolate cake is owned by the family of Elijah Moe in Charleston, South Carolina; its secret is a precise baking time that leaves the center between solid and liquid.
Uncle Moe's instructions call for bittersweet chocolate with a minimum of 70% cocoa; the secret was first decoded on an October evening in 2023.
Betty Griffin's Billionaire Bars layer buttery shortbread, salted caramel, and silky chocolate, and are a sensation in Greenville, Mississippi.
The Billionaire Bars' ratios have been perfected since their inception on November 16, 2023, and Betty's niece Jane Griffin measures each ingredient with scientific precision.
Uncle John's gingersnaps have been part of the Perry household in Topeka, Kansas every holiday season since 2024, baked in Terry Perry's oven.
The gingersnaps' trick is blackstrap molasses plus a trifecta of powdered, fresh, and candied ginger, giving a distinctive snap.
Aunt Marie's bread pudding is made in Bedford-Stuyvesant by her great-grandson David, using vanilla bean custard and staled challah as a nod to the family's Jewish heritage.
Marie's technique of letting the bread soak up the custard overnight is non-negotiable.
Sister Emma's apple dumplings come from the Appalachian foothills, where Emma and her brother Louis Thompson perfected them one frigid December morning in 2023.
The apple dumplings use locally sourced Granny Smith apples in tender pastry with a cinnamon-spiced sauce, and are made special by being prepared together.
